name: Neroli

card.summary: A floral essential oil distilled from bitter orange blossoms, used as a fragrance and skin-care ingredient to add a pleasant natural scent to a grooming routine.
card.aka: neroli oil, orange blossom oil, Citrus aurantium amara flower oil
card.note: Contains terpenes that can sensitize skin in some people.

quick.overview:
Neroli is an essential oil steam-distilled from the blossoms of the bitter orange tree. It smells sweet, honeyed and slightly green, and is one of the most widely used floral notes in perfumery.

For appearance, it matters as part of grooming: it features in colognes, body and face products and moisturizers, so that a person presents a pleasant scent along with a polished look. Studies of the oil itself concern aromatherapy and anxiety, not skin or looks.
quick.how: People encounter neroli as a note in fragrances or as an ingredient in creams, toners, hydrosols and bath products. Some use diluted oil or neroli-scented products for relaxation. Forum mentions are occasional, for example in moisturizer threads.
quick.risks: The oil contains linalool, limonene, geraniol and citral, terpenes that can cause skin sensitization in some people, so it is usually used diluted in finished products. Patch testing is a common precaution cited for essential oils generally.

lead: Neroli is the essential oil obtained by steam distillation of the blossoms of the bitter orange tree, Citrus aurantium subsp. amara. Blossoms are usually picked by hand in spring, and Tunisia, Morocco and Egypt are leading producers [2]. It is described as sweet, honeyed and slightly spicy, and blends easily with citrus and other floral materials [2].

In looksmaxxing and grooming it works as a scent and as a cosmetic ingredient: it appears in perfumes and in skin-care products, contributing to a well-kept impression through fragrance. The name dates to the late 17th century, when Anne Marie Orsini, Princess of Nerola, used bitter orange essence to scent her gloves and bath [2].

Published research on neroli concerns mood and aromatherapy: small randomized trials have looked at neroli-scented products and anxiety, and reviews cover citrus essential oils generally [1][3]. No study has examined neroli for facial appearance.

chain: Neroli added to perfume or skin products
angle.text: Neroli adds a fresh floral scent to colognes and skin-care products. People use it as part of a grooming routine; the effect is on fragrance and perceived freshness, not on the skin itself.

paras: Neroli oil is steam-distilled from hand-picked bitter orange blossoms [2]. Its aroma comes from terpenes including linalool and limonene, which are also the constituents that may sensitize skin [2]. Chemical analyses of regional oils, such as Egyptian neroli, report their composition [4].
Neroli is among the most used floral oils in perfume [2]. Forum users sometimes mention neroli-scented products in discussions of moisturizers, where it is one of several fragrance choices.

A review of citrus essential oils summarizes the biological activities and safety of neroli alongside sweet orange, bergamot and others [1]. Randomized trials have examined inhaled or chewed neroli products on anxiety, including a 72-student chewing gum study [5]. These studies concern mood, not looks.
No studies found on neroli for skin or appearance. Trials exist on aromatherapy and anxiety [5]; see above.

timeline.event: Anne Marie Orsini, Princess of Nerola, scents gloves and bath with bitter orange essence, giving neroli its name [2].
